UKIP’s 2015 manifesto is a call to believe in Britain: to leave the EU, restore sovereignty over our laws, borders and money, and redirect waste into frontline priorities without raising taxes or debt. It pledges fully costed, common‑sense reforms that put British citizens first.

Spending and tax
- Leave the EU, saving £9bn a year; scrap HS2; cut foreign aid to 0.2% of GNI; replace the unfair Barnett formula; slim Whitehall and quangos. Use the savings to invest an extra £12bn in the NHS and £5.2bn in social care, plus more police, prisons and border staff.
- Make work pay: raise the personal allowance to at least £13,000 (taking minimum‑wage earners out of income tax), raise the 40% threshold to £55,000 with a new 30% band, scrap inheritance tax, expand the married couple’s transferable allowance, and cut small business rates.
- Regain tax sovereignty to stop multinationals’ avoidance; gain VAT control (e.g., remove VAT from sanitary products and listed‑building repairs).

Immigration and borders
- End EU free movement by leaving the EU; introduce an Australian‑style points system; five‑year moratorium on unskilled migration; equal rules for all nationalities.
- +2,500 Border Agency staff; count all in/out; no amnesty; fast‑track removal of foreign criminals; five years’ tax/NI before access to benefits or non‑urgent NHS.

NHS and social care
- Keep the NHS free at the point of need; recruit 8,000 GPs, 20,000 nurses, 3,000 midwives; GP triage in A&E; £1.5bn for mental health and dementia; free hospital parking.
- End health tourism via mandatory insurance; protect the NHS from TTIP; scrap harmful EU directives; integrate health and social care; restore £1.2bn/yr to social care; dignity code; +£572 for carers.

Education, skills, families
- More school choice including grammar, technical and vocational routes; abolish Key Stage 1 SATs; cut teacher workload; age‑appropriate sex education.
- Presumption of 50:50 shared parenting; overhaul child protection.
- Waive tuition fees for UK students in STEMM and medicine who work in the UK for five years; tighten international student abuse; expand wraparound childcare 8am–6pm and deregulate to increase affordable places.

Housing and environment
- Build on brownfield (national register, remediation grants), remove stamp duty up to £250k for new brownfield homes, bring empties back into use; prioritize locals/5‑year contributors for social housing; protect green belt.
- Cut fuel bills: scrap green levies/ETS; back secure, affordable energy—shale gas with safeguards, modern coal and nuclear; support hydro; end wind/solar subsidies.

Law, order and justice
- 6,000 extra frontline posts across police, prisons and borders; leave ECHR; UK Bill of Rights; restore “innocent until proven guilty”; curb EU justice measures.
- Zero tolerance of FGM, forced marriage and honour crimes; decriminalize TV licence non‑payment.

Defence and foreign affairs
- Meet and exceed 2% of GDP on defence; retain Trident; rebuild forces; tax‑free pay on operations; oppose an EU army.
- “Trade not aid”: cut/retarget aid to emergencies, clean water, vaccinations; close DFID and fold essentials into the FCO.

Jobs and small business
- Prioritize British workers; enforce minimum wage; fair zero‑hours code; punish late‑paying big firms; pilot trade‑credit insurance; 30‑minute free town‑centre parking.

Farming, fishing, heritage
- UK Single Farm Payment favouring family farms; honest food labelling; stronger animal welfare; ban live exports.
- Leave the CFP; 12‑mile UK zone and 200‑mile EEZ; protect small boats and sea angling.
- Protect heritage, remove VAT on listed‑building repairs, revive seaside towns; save British pubs.

Political and local reform
- Citizens’ Initiative referendums; real Recall of MPs; confirmation and expenditure hearings to hold government to account; proportional voting with a constituency link; clean up postal voting; empower local referenda; weekly bins.
- Celebrate British culture, language and values; bank holidays for St George’s and St David’s Days.

We think NHS managers should be subject to disciplinary oversight in the same way as doctors and nurses who are regulated by the General Medical Council and the Nursing and Midwifery Council. There are no clear national statistics to tell us how many people are homeless in the UK. UKIP will encourage moves by local authorities to prioritise people with strong local connections when making housing allocations. Right to Buy and Help to Buy
UKIP supports the principle of extending home ownership and giving people the right to own the homes they may have lived in for generations as social housing tenants. We will plough 100 per cent of all revenue from Right to Buy sales, after essential costs have been paid back, into new community housing.

Given that Britain’s social housing stock is so massively oversubscribed, we do not believe it is either sensible or fair to give foreign nationals the opportunity to obtain social housing stock, buy their home at a discount and then sell it for an untaxed profit before moving back abroad. The ‘three Million Jobs’ Myth
Finally, a word on the pernicious myth that leaving the EU will cost three million British jobs. This myth grew out of a report by the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) in 2000, which concluded that 2.7 million jobs were directly related to our trade with the EU and another 500,000 were indirectly linked. This is our roadmap to freedom: the process that will lead Great Britain out of the EU and into the world.

A Referendum on Membership
UKIP believes British citizens should have an in/out referendum on our membership of the EU as soon as possible. Our question of choice will be:

Do You Wish Britain to Be a Free, Independent, Sovereign Democracy?
Only British citizens will be allowed to vote and there will be strict spending limits for both ‘yes’ and ‘no’ camps, together with fair, balanced and equal media coverage of both arguments. Following a vote to leave, we have two legal options:

We repeal the European Communities Act 1972 and
leave immediately

We activate Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty and notify
the European Council that the UK has decided to leave the EU in two years’ time. The second option provides for a sensible, orderly exit and this is the option we prefer.

Preparation for Withdrawal from the EU
Having activated Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty, we will set a fixed date, two years ahead, on which we intend to leave, while recognising we could leave earlier. Then we will begin amicable negotiations. British exit will be a huge relief for many other EU members, who have known all along that the vast majority of the British people find the idea of political union with the rest of Europe abhorrent. They are fully aware that we would never have joined the EU, had the political nature of the enterprise not been deliberately concealed from the electorate in 1975.

Our leaving will set them free to have full political union, if that is what they really want and set us free to make the most of all our links with the Commonwealth, with North America, Australasia, much of Africa, the Indian sub- continent and all the other countries where English is the first or second language, as well as, of course, with Europe and the EU itself. The UK is the EU’s largest export market and, militarily, the strongest European member of NATO. With Russia once more flexing its muscles and controlling much of the energy supplies to Western Europe, the other EU member states will have more than a casual interest in making sure their relationship with us remains amicable.

Agreeing Brexit: the Objectives
What do we wish to achieve from our negotiations with the EU? Our objectives are clear: Firstly, we will secure trade agreements with the EU, the 40 nations with trade agreements with the EU and other nations of interest to us. As a G7 member, a leading world economy, the fifth largest by GDP, this will be a rapid process in most cases. Countries already trading with the EU will want to continue seamless trade relationships; other world nations will want to forge new trade alliances with the UK; and all nations will find it easier to deal with the UK directly.

As a minimum, we will seek continued access on free-trade terms to the EU’s single market. Our custom is valuable to the EU now and will continue to be so following Brexit. Secondly, there will be a wide range of issues on which we will want to continue to co-operate. These include extradition treaties, cross-border intelligence, disaster relief, accommodation of refugees, pan-EU healthcare arrangements and various other cultural projects. We will also maintain our membership of pan-European institutions, such as the European Space Agency and the European Medicines Agency.
